title: TA9-21597
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXX (the claimant), a citizen of the People's Republic of China, claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
Subsequent to the hearing of the claim, the panel received counsel's written submissions on September 16th, 2011.

The claimant alleged that after she and her husband divorced in 2005, her health deteriorated because of the stress of being a single parent. Then, in XXXXXX 2008 the claimant had a sudden dizzy spell and fell down bumping her head. She went to hospital for treatment. The claimant's friend, XXXXX, learned of this and came to her bedside to pray for her. Later, she introduced the claimant to an underground Roman Catholic church in her home area of XXXXX, Fujian province. The claimant attended this church every week from September 2008 until it was raided by the Public Security Bureau (PSB) on XXXXX, 2009.

The claimant was late because of the bus on the day the church was raided, but when she saw the police vehicles near the house church location she went into hiding. Subsequently she learned that the PSB went to her home to look for her, they questioned her brother, and accused her of being involved in illegal religious activities. She also found out that three members of her congregation had been arrested, including XXXXX, and when the claimant failed to report to the PSB a summons was sent to the claimant's home for her to comply.

The PSB has kept coming to her home to look for her. The claimant fears that if she returned to China she would be arrested and jailed, and she adds that she cannot practice her religion as freely in China as she can in Canada.
In an addendum2 to her Personal Information Form3 (PIF) narrative, she stated that in XXX XXXXX 2009 she learned that the three persons arrested were each sentenced to three years imprisonment.

The claimant's identity as a national of the People's Republic of China is established by documentation provided to the panel by the claimant, specifically, the Chinese Resident Identity Card (RIC),4 and passport5 as tendered into evidence.
The panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee and is not a person in need of protection for the following reasons.

The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's PIF6 narrative and oral testimony concerning the claimant's membership in an underground church and her pursuit by agents of the PSB. I find that the claimant was not a credible witness in this regard and is not currently wanted for arrest by the PSB on account of her religious activities in China. As well, I find that should she return to her home in Fujian province in China and should she practice Roman Catholicism there, there is not a serious possibility that she would be persecuted in Fujian province for that practice. The reasons for this decision are noted below.

In assessing credibility, the panel was mindful of the claimant's age, education, and background in China. She alleges that she has fourteen years of education in China. In addition, the panel took into account the milieu of the hearing room, cultural factors, and the anxiety a claimant may feel in responding to viva voce examination through an interpreter. The dates of PSB visits and when the claimant learned they were looking for her

The claimant testified that she last went to attend at her church on XXXXX, 2009, but then she immediately went to her aunt's home to hide. While there, she learned from her aunt that the PSB were looking for her. I asked when she had learned of this, and she replied that her aunt told her at the end of XXX, around the XXX. She added that her elder brother had informed her aunt after the PSB first went to her home on XXXXX to look for her, and talked to him. Then, the PSB returned on XXXXX and also on the XXX. She testified that the summons was left with her brother on the XXX.

I noted to the claimant that her PIF narrative specified that the summons was only issued after she had failed to report, as requested by the PSB during their first visit. It states,7 "When I failed to report to the PSB a summons was issued...." However, if that was correct then it could not have been left with her brother on the XXX. She replied that she believed that there was something wrong with the original Chinese documentation. The "Notice of Summoning"8 is dated XXXXX, 2009 and summoned the claimant to appear on XXXXX, 2009.

I pointed out to her that if her oral testimony about the sequence of PSB visits was correct, then the summons could not have been left until XXXXX, yet it was dated XXXXX. She replied that she thought there was a difference between her written PIF narrative and her Chinese written document.
I asked why her PIF narrative did not mention any dates after that of the XXXXX PSB raid, and she replied that at the time she did not put all the details.

It is apparent that there is an important discrepancy in the claimant's testimony about the dates and sequence of events which she was unable to explain. I draw a negative credibility inference as a result. Moreover, I draw a negative inference from the omission from her narrative of the date details regarding when the PSB first went to look for her and when she learned of this. Such matters are central to the claim as they would establish when the authorities targeted her, and when she learned that her fear was tangible. The PIF narrative instructions specify that one should set out all the significant reasons that have led you to claim refugee protection. I would expect that the narrative should have given the precise event dates, and when she found out.

This area of testimony concerned me, so I asked the claimant a second time to state when she had learned of PSB interest in herself personally. She said that on XXXXX her aunt had told her this, as the claimant's brother had been in telephone contact with the aunt. I noted to her that her earlier oral testimony had been that she learned that the PSB were looking for her at the end of XXX, on the XXX, and this was not consistent with her current answer.
She said that she was sorry, and that she was confused.

Again, the claimant's testimony about important dates was inconsistent and confused, when one would reasonably expect that if such events had actually happened, then testimony should have been straightforward. I draw a further negative credibility inference. Delay in leaving China

The claimant testified that she met a snakehead or agent at the end of XXX, around XXXX. I noted to her that her passport contained a United States visa, dated XXXX, 2009,9 and asked why she did not leave China right away. She said that the snakehead told her that they had a certain route to go to Canada, and Canada had religious freedom.

I noted to her that it was within my specialized knowledge that the United States accepted asylum claims from Chinese claimants, so I was puzzled why she would delay leaving China if she had a valid United States visitor visa. By comparison, her Canadian visa10 was not issued until XXXXXX, 2009, about eleven weeks later, and she only left China on XXXXXXXX, 2009.11 The successful Canadian visa application refers to a previous unsuccessful application.12
She said that the snakehead had not mentioned where she would go, he held her passport, and determined when she would leave.

While I note the claimant's answer, I weigh this against the clear fact that her passport had a valid United States visa in early XXX, but she did not leave until XXXXXXXX, three and a half months later. If she truly feared being arrested by the PSB starting in XXXXX, one would expect that she would want to leave China as soon as possible on any reasonable basis to avoid her stated fear of arrest and detention, and would have given precise and specific instructions to that effect. It is not enough for her to say that she entrusted everything to an agent.

One would also expect that agents, being rational, would wish to limit delay, as it would be bad for business to lose too many customers to PSB arrest, and might conceivably also lead to their own incarceration.
As a result of the significant delay in leaving China, I draw a negative inference regarding her subjective fear and also her credibility. The PSB Summons

The claimant also entered a document entitled, "Notice of Summoning"13 that she has alleged was left with her family after the raid on her church group. The documentary evidence14 regarding the issuance of a summons notes that a summons would almost always be issued to the individual rather than a household or family member. However, it was also noted that it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave the summons with family members, instructing them to pass it along to the person named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgment of receipt. Though this is not actually the proper procedure it happens all the time, especially in cases when a person in the summons is not easily locatable. The documentary evidence15 also notes the format and appearance of summonses. It is stated that the notice is prepared in triplicate. The original is kept at the police station, the duplicate copy is signed, dated and returned by the suspect and one copy is left with the suspect. The summons presented by the claimant at her hearing includes no section that is an acknowledgment that the summons was received. This is not consistent with the documentary evidence. As noted above, a summons is either issued to the person named in the summons or to a family or household member and the person who receives the summons is expected to sign in that regard. There is no signature or acknowledgment of receipt of any kind on the summons provided by the claimant.

Furthermore, I note that the claimant's summons did not identify her address, age or gender, or acknowledgement of service on the face of the document, which is not consistent with the sample document in the National Documentation Package.16 The claimant was given an opportunity to explain why the PSB Summons lacked these features and responded, "I don't know."

I have also considered the statement in Response to Information Request CHN42444.E17 (the "RIR") which identifies the types of summonses: Zhaunhaun, which is used to summon a suspect for questioning without arrest, and Juzhaun, an arrest-summons. The RIR states the Zhaunhaun summons for someone to appear for interrogation must state the person, time, and place of appearance for questioning. The duplicate copy is signed, dated and returned by the suspect who keeps one copy. The same RIR goes on to attach samples of an arrest warrant (Juliu Zheng), an arrest-summons for interrogation (Juzhuan Zheng), and a notice of summons to testify or Zhaunhuan Tongzhishu summons.18

The claimant testified that the police only left the summons with her brother after they had informed him during a previous visit that his sister was accused of being involved in illegal religious activities, ordered her to report and she had failed to do so, and other church members had been arrested already.

According to the RIR, Zhuanhuan (summons) is used when no arrest or detention of suspects is necessary or contemplated, i.e. when cooperation is expected or flight is not likely. See Article 92 of PRC Criminal Procedure Law. This is not a coercive measure (qiang zhi cuoshi ). (Emphasis added). However, the claimant's testimony would suggest that her arrest was both necessary and contemplated by the PSB, and she had not reported as requested in their first visit, so in my view this would rule out use of the Zhuanhuan.
The Notice of Summmoning submitted by the claimant also refers to article 92 of the PRC Criminal Law, as does the sample for Zhuanhuan.

I do not think that the PSB would possibly have used a Zhuanhuan in circumstances as describe by the claimant. Instead, a Juzhuan (arrest summons) would most likely be used in such circumstances "when voluntary compliance is not appropriate or zhuanhuan has failed. See Article 50 of PRC Criminal Procedure Law and Article 60 of Public Security Criminal Procedure Regulations. This is a coercive measure (qiang zhi cuoshi )."19 Also, the Juzhuan refers not to Article 92, but to Article 45.
Claimant's counsel submitted that there may be substantial differences in the type of information on the summonses issued by various PSB offices.

I give little weight to this submission since I note that the claimant is from XXXX, Fujian province which is a county-level city of suburban Fuzhou, the capital and largest city in Fujian. Fuzhou has an urban population of approximately seven million people. It is reasonable to assume that the police force of a large and populous area such as this would be well versed with regard to the information that would be required for the effective service and procedures associated with the issuance of summonses. By relying on common sense and rationale, in my opinion, it is reasonable to assume that the PSB document would include the address of the person named on the summons, their age and gender, and an acknowledgement of service, since this information would be required by the serving officer(s) to correctly identify the individual and the location of the individual's known address to effect service of the document.

The Panel determines that it is neither reasonable nor credible that the summons would not identify the claimant's address, age, and gender on the face of the document since it is the only way the serving PSB officer(s) could identify the claimant and the actual location that they were to attend in search of her as well as serve the summons. Further, it is neither reasonable nor credible that the summons would not have an acknowledgement of service. As well, it is neither reasonable nor credible to the panel that the document submitted by the claimant cites the Chinese Criminal Law article pertaining to a notice of summons to testify or Zhaunhuan Tongzhishu, and not that for an arrest-summons for interrogation (Juzhuan Zheng), when the latter is clearly appropriate in the circumstances and the former is not.
I note from the documentary evidence that fraudulent documents, including summonses are easily acquired in China.20

I have considered the inconsistencies in the summons provided by the claimant compared to the documentary evidence, as well as the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China and I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the summons provided by the claimant is not a genuine document and the claimant has deliberately attempted to mislead the panel by proffering a fraudulent document as evidence to support her refugee claim and substantiate her PIF narrative.

For these same reasons, I further determine that the claimant is not wanted by the PSB for any alleged involvement in any underground church practice. I note that this specific analysis regarding deficiencies in PSB summons documents has recently been considered by the Federal Court in two separate instances and found not to be unreasonable.21 Arrests of others

The claimant alleges that three of her fellow church members were arrested and each received multi-year sentences. The claimant's testimony in this regard runs counter to the country condition documents, which will be demonstrated later in these reasons with the analysis of the Situation of Catholics in Fujian Province. I draw a negative inference as a result.

On the basis of the subsequent analysis on the Situation of Catholics in Fujian Province and in the context of the findings and negative inferences drawn above, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities that the claimant's allegation that there was a raid on her house church and that three of her fellow church members were arrested and each received multi-year sentences is neither plausible nor credible. Having found that the claimant's testimony about the arrest and incarceration of her fellow church members is not credible, the panel further finds that the alleged raid on the claimant's house church did not occur.

The claimant was asked a number of questions concerning Catholicism and the Bible. The claimant demonstrated some limited knowledge, however it does not necessarily mean she is a genuine practicing Catholic. Claimant's Canadian Church Attendance

The claimant alleges that shortly after arriving in Canada she joined Chinese Martyrs Catholic Church. The claimant produced a letter from Rev. XXXX and some photographs,22 as well as a baptismal certificate.23 The letter indicates that the claimant has been attending church since 2009. These documents can only attest to the claimant's participation in church activities, they can not attest to her true motivation.

While it is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a person's religious practice, it is necessary in this case. In doing so, the panel considered the totality of the evidence available. While it is true that the claimant demonstrated some knowledge of Roman Catholicism, it does not necessarily mean she is a genuine practicing Roman Catholic. Having previously found that the raid on the claimant's underground church did not occur, the panel finds that the claimant's testimony concerning her attendance at the underground church was not credible and was only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim.
Having found that the claimant was not a practicing Catholic in China, the panel must consider whether the claimant is a genuine practicing Catholic in this country.

In this regard, the panel cites the following from James Hathaway's The Law of Refugee Status with regard to "sur place" claims: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution, which did not exist, cannot be said to belong to this category.24 The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of all of findings and negative inference drawn above, that this claim has not been made in good faith.

Having found that the claimant was not a genuine practicing Roman Catholic in China and having found that this claim has not been made in good faith, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of the findings noted above, that the claimant joined a Roman Catholic church in Canada only for the purpose of furthering her refugee claim. In the context as noted above, and on the basis of the totality of evidence disclosed and in the context of the claimant's knowledge of Roman Catholicism, the panel finds that the claimant is not a genuine practicing Roman Catholic, nor would she be perceived to be in China. Situation of Catholics in Fujian Province

Notwithstanding the forgoing analysis, alternatively, if the claimant decides to become a genuine Catholic and practice her faith upon her return to China, the panel has considered whether there is a serious possibility that she would be persecuted for practicing Catholicism in an unregistered church.

In dealing with the issue of repression of Catholics in Fujian province, the panel has examined the documentary evidence closely. Although precise figures are difficult to obtain, documentation25 highlights: The Catholic Patriotic Association (CPA) reports that 5.3 million persons worship in its churches, and it is estimated that there are an additional 12 million or more persons who worship in unregistered Catholic churches that do not affiliate with the CPA. According to official sources, the government-sanctioned Catholic Patriotic Association has more than 70 bishops, almost 3,000 priests and nuns, 6,000 churches and meeting places, and 12 seminaries. There are thought to be approximately 40 bishops operating "underground," some of whom are in prison or under house arrest.

With respect to Fujian province, where the claimant is from, according to a report in the Times of London, the Catholic Church is strong there and most of the faithful are loyal to Rome.26 The panel acknowledges that sporadic persecution of the "underground" Catholic Church occurs. There are references to Catholic clergy being forced into hiding, jailed or detained, placed under surveillance and detentions, pressure being applied by Chinese authorities for Catholic clergy and laypersons to renounce ordinations approved by the Vatican and join the CPA or face fines, job loss, or detention and having children barred from school.27 According to one source as of March 2007, five bishops and 14 priests belonging to the "underground" church were in prison, eight bishops were under house arrest or surveillance and two others were in hiding.28 The documentation29 identifies that the treatment of Catholics, within the "unofficial" church, varies from place to place. It is local politics that dictate the final outcome of religious policy and the implementation of the Chinese Communist Party on freedom of religious belief can range from endorsement of religion to suppression.

There is mixed information regarding the treatment of Christians in Fujian province. Several sources stated that they believed that authorities in Guangdong and Fujian provinces might be more tolerant than those in other Chinese provinces. The Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council expressed the opinion that officials in Guangdong and Fujian provinces have good relations with government-recognized bishops and have allowed non-official bishops to operate openly.30 Conversely, a newspaper article refers to Fujian as one of the provinces where the most Catholics are located and that they are [translation] "tightly controlled" by local authorities. The President of the Cardinal Kung Foundation stated that Fujian province was one of "the worst" provinces for the "persecution" of the unofficial Catholic Church.

There are no diplomatic relationships existing currently between the Chinese Government and the Holy See. It is estimated that 90 percent of official Catholic bishops have reconciled with the Vatican. Many priests and bishops publicly acknowledged that the Vatican had approved their appointments. They suffered no punishment for this public stance. Pressure from the CPA on "unregistered" Catholic bishops to join the official church continued, and some unregistered priests and bishops were detained.

The State has declared that religious communities are important for the construction of a "harmonious society." From the perspective of the Holy See, there has been no declaration of a schism between any part of the Catholic Church in China and the Vatican.31 This is not to suggest that tensions do not exist between the Chinese government and the Holy See. Contentious issues surrounding the government's control of the selection of "patriotic" Chinese bishops and local officials cracking down on the "underground" church remain.

The panel is mindful that certain documentation32 indicates that the number of persecutory incidents may not be fully reflected in documentation and such factors as censorship in communications, failure to report cases of persecution for fear of retaliation by the government and the possibility that individuals in remote areas may have no idea that they can seek help from outside China can effect the number of reports.

In the case of the Catholic Church, there is information detailing very specific examples from areas much more remote and difficult to access than Fujian province. There is even information from Fujian province that indicates to the panel that information regarding persecutory treatment against members of the Catholic faith is documented if it has occurred. Further, there are a number of observers, such as the Holy Spirit Study Centre, the Research Branch of the Diocese of Hong Kong (principally concerned with the situation of Catholics in mainland China), AsiaNews.it (which provides information on ecclesiastic communities in Asia), numerous news agencies, Cardinal Fung Foundation, and Freedom House33 to name a few. These observers strive to inform the world whenever any religious persecution takes place in China.
Arguably, the Roman Catholic Church itself has a vested interest in bringing to light any abhorrent human rights transgressions involving its adherents.

In the 9 June 2010 telephone interview with the IRB Research Directorate,34 Mr. Bob Fu, "the President of China Aid Association stated that east coast provinces are generally 'more open' with fewer incidents involving Christians reported to the CAA (CAA 9 June 2010). However, the CAA President also stated that this did not necessarily mean there were fewer incidents, but rather that they were not reported (ibid.)."

In reference to the claimant's particular allegations, in the panel's view, if three arrests with multi-year jail sentences of Roman Catholic Churchgoers had occurred, such would be an example of an egregious situation and would reasonably be expected to appear in reports dealing with religious persecution amongst the multitude of different sources, which strive to inform the world of religious repression in China.

Given that information can flow to and from mainland China via means of personal contact, informal NGO networks, telephone calls, etc.; and, that in the past, there has been documentary evidence dealing with detention and arrests of Catholic bishops and priests, from Fujian and other more remote provinces; and, because of the large number of documentary sources that have a vested interest in highlighting any and all information that negatively impacts on religious freedom, the panel determines that it would be reasonable for it to have before it information of state actions taken against Catholic parishioners in Fujian province if any actions were taken.

The most recent documentary35 evidence provided by the Board reveals that underground priests have been arrested in Fujian in March 2010. Given the fact that information exists to show arrests of priests, it is reasonable to expect to see persuasive evidence that ordinary members of the Roman Catholic Church in Fujian province are facing persecution. Further, the availability of priests, nuns and lay catechists in the diocese associated with Fujian province persuades the panel that the claimant can return to Fujian and participate in the Roman Catholic church of her choosing.

The claimant testified that three fellow house church members were arrested and were ultimately sentenced to multi-year imprisonment. A close examination of the documentation regarding Catholic faithful in China clearly indicates that the harshest treatment is meted out to Bishops and Priests. In the case of Fujian province the most recent article indicates that the priests involved in organizing the camp for three hundred university students were detained for fifteen days and then released. Other priests involved in the matter were fined 500 Yuan. In terms of the totality of the evidence the alleged punishment given to the three lay members of the claimant's church, who were arrested, is not in keeping with the types of punishment that has been referred to in the documentation with respect to non-Priests or Bishops.

Relying on documentary evidence that indicates millions of Catholic parishioners belong to the "unregistered" church and that the documentation in the context of the "unregistered" Catholic Church indicates, by far, that persecution occurs to bishops and priests. Further, there is extremely limited evidence of state authorities taking action against parishioners in Fujian province. In addition, Catholic congregations, worship freely. It is reasonable to expect that documentation from Fujian province indicating actions by state authorities against parishioners at the time of the alleged incident and more recently should be before the panel. In coming to this determination, the panel has been guided by the Federal Court decisions in Yu,36 Li,37 and Zhang38

Based of the totality of findings noted above, the panel determines that the claimant has not satisfied her burden of establishing a serious possibility that she would be persecuted or that she would be personally subjected to a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects her claim.
